demoTitle: Can GenAI Predict Code's Energy Use and Why Should We Care?

steps.content: Sparky, what is this demo about?

We use GenAI to spot energy waste in real Java libraries.
Same behavior. Less CPU. Lower CO2.
Why does code waste energy in the first place?

Hidden work: buffer resizing, idle polling, repeated copies.
Small loops × huge scale = real electricity.
How do you measure it?

Count micro-ops → estimate mWh → multiply by grid carbon intensity.
Not exact. Repeatable enough to compare.
Show us the first real example.

Library: JSON-java — used by millions of projects.
Method: JSONObject.toString()
Every call starts with an undersized buffer.
What does the waste look like?

The StringBuilderWriter starts empty, grows during serialization.
Each resize = wasted allocation and copy work.

code.caption: Annotated hotspot — ~280 uOps total per call
code.intro: JSONObject.toString() is the main JSON serialization entry point. It creates a Writer, calls write() recursively over all key-value pairs, then returns the assembled JSON string. Called on every serialization.

steps.content: What did GenAI suggest?
Pre-size the writer based on map entries. One estimate, zero mid-write resizes.

code.caption: PR diff — pre-size the writer
code.intro: Same toString() method. The fix adds a capacity hint to StringBuilderWriter so the internal char[] is right-sized before serialization begins.
code.why: Starting empty forces the buffer to grow 3× on average. Pre-sizing from map.size() × 6 eliminates all mid-write reallocations and the copy work they trigger.

steps.content: Next — any pointless search loops?

Annotation lookup walked every superclass — even past Object.
Early exit was missing.

code.caption: PR diff — stop the walk at Object
code.intro: getAnnotation() walks the class hierarchy to find a matching annotation. Without a guard, the loop always climbs past java.lang.Object even though Object carries no user-defined annotations.
code.why: Without the check, the loop always reaches java.lang.Object and continues one extra level unnecessarily. One null-check stops the walk as soon as no more annotations are possible.
code.energySaving: ~60 uOps saved per lookup · scales with call frequency

steps.content: Simple fix — big difference?

One null-check saves ~60 uOps per lookup.
At library scale that path runs millions of times.
What about deeply nested XML input?

No depth cap → recursive parser runs forever on crafted input.
CPU held hostage.

code.caption: PR diff — fail fast on depth exceeded
code.intro: XML.parse() is a recursive descent parser that converts XML to JSONObject. Each nested element opens a new stack frame. Without a depth limit, a deeply nested document can exhaust CPU and stack.
code.why: Deeply nested XML is O(depth) in recursion. Without a cap, a crafted 10,000-level document monopolises the worker thread. The depth check throws early and releases the CPU immediately.
code.energySaving: Prevents unbounded CPU use — worst-case O(n) → O(1) at depth limit

steps.content: Any duplicate conversion work in JSON-java?

String-to-number logic lived in multiple places.
Every caller paid the parse cost independently.

code.caption: PR diff — one conversion path via utility
code.intro: stringToNumber() converts a JSON numeric string (e.g. "3.14") to the correct Java Number subtype. It was implemented both directly in JSONObject and in coercion helpers — two copies of the same parse logic.
code.why: Duplicate logic means the same string gets parsed multiple times per access. Routing through NumberConversionUtil lets the JIT inline and optimise a single hot path instead of two.
code.energySaving: ~120 uOps · ~0.00004 mWh — paid once instead of per call-site

steps.content: Show us the idle waiting pattern.

Each Tailer spawned its own thread.
Idle watchers still wake, poll file size, sleep — on repeat.
At scale: background CPU for nothing.
What does the polling loop look like?
Thread wakes, checks file size, finds nothing, sleeps — again.

code.caption: Before — per-instance thread + sleep loop
code.intro: Tailer.run() is the main polling loop for the unix-tail equivalent. It repeatedly reads new lines from a growing file and notifies a TailerListener. The old implementation gave each Tailer its own OS thread that woke on a fixed sleep interval regardless of file activity.

steps.content: What is the fix?
Replace per-instance thread with a shared ScheduledExecutor.

code.caption: PR diff — ScheduledExecutor replaces the sleep loop
code.intro: The new run() delegates scheduling to a ScheduledExecutorService. The method blocks on a CountDownLatch instead of looping, and the executor handles the fixed-delay firing.
code.why: Each dedicated thread consumes ~140 uOps of infrastructure just to exist. A shared ScheduledExecutor amortises that cost across all tailers and only wakes threads when work is actually due.
code.energySaving: ~140 uOps thread overhead eliminated + ~35 uOps × idle polls removed

steps.content: Parser work — what did GenAI find in Jackson?

readString() materialised a text snapshot before streaming it.
Direct streaming skips the intermediate copy.

code.caption: PR diff — tighten exception scope, add reusable buffer
code.intro: ReaderBasedJsonParser.readString(Writer) streams the current JSON string token directly into a caller-supplied Writer, bypassing string materialisation. It is the fast path for processing large string values without heap allocation.
code.why: The original try-catch wrapped the entire VALUE_STRING branch, preventing the JIT from hoisting the token check outside the exception range. Narrowing the scope lets the happy path run without exception-table overhead; the reusable buffer avoids 100k+ temp array allocations.
code.energySaving: ~90 uOps hot path · reusable buffer saves ~3.5M uOps per 100k calls

steps.content: Any string decoding that gets thrown away?

resetWithASCII() decoded a String then returned void.
Callers fetched it again — paid twice.

code.caption: PR diff — return the decoded String directly
code.intro: TextBuffer.resetWithASCII() reinitialises the buffer with a pre-decoded ASCII/Latin-1 byte array. It is called on every JSON string token that can be decoded without escaping. The result is used by all callers as the token's string value.
code.why: The decode step (~140 uOps) already produces the String object. Returning void forced every caller to invoke getText() as a follow-up, adding ~4–8 uOps per call. Returning the value directly removes that dead round-trip.
code.energySaving: ~140 uOps decode reused · ~4–8 uOps follow-up eliminated per call

steps.content: What about logging overhead?

Every log event copies the thread context map.
The generic HashMap(Map) constructor hides a megamorphic call.
Hot path. Runs constantly.
Show the getCopy fix.
Pre-size the target map. Iterate explicitly. JIT loves predictable paths.

code.caption: PR diff — explicit pre-sized copy
code.intro: DefaultThreadContextMap.getCopy() returns a snapshot of the current thread's MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) map. It is called on every log event that uses context fields — potentially thousands of times per second in a busy application.
code.why: HashMap(Map) uses a megamorphic copy path that the JIT cannot easily optimise. Pre-sizing with load-factor headroom (×1.35) eliminates the first resize, and explicit entry iteration gives the JIT a monomorphic loop it can inline and vectorise.
code.energySaving: ~25 uOps resize saved · ~30 uOps/iter × 100k iters = 3.0M uOps total

steps.content: How do we put this into practice?

Eight patterns to look for:
- Right-size buffers upfront
- Add early exits to search loops
- Cap recursive depth
- Centralize repeated conversions
- Replace polling with events
- Stream instead of buffering
- Return decoded values, don't re-fetch
- Pre-size copies, iterate explicitly
Where does GenAI fit in this workflow?

Run the lens on changed files in CI.
Annotate likely hotspots. Flag the pattern.
Require a human decision: accept, mitigate, or justify.
Give the audience one takeaway.

Better software wastes less.
Same behavior. Less CPU. Lower CO2.
GenAI shows you where to look — you decide what to fix.
